learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A young woman walks in with three days of fever and headache. Decide what to ask, what to test, and what to treat — the way you would on a busy morning.
objectives: Recognise danger signs that change a febrile presentation from routine to urgent
Apply the test-before-treat rule for suspected malaria (Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023)
Dose artemether-lumefantrine by weight, and counsel on completing the course
Choose the correct HMIS diagnosis after a positive RDT
takeaways: Fever ≥ 38 °C with headache earns a deliberate danger-sign screen first.
Test before you treat — a positive RDT comes before antimalarials.
AL at ≥ 35 kg: 4 tablets twice daily for 3 days. Finish the course.
Code the confirmed diagnosis (B54), not the presenting symptom.

coach.title: Grace is next in the queue
coach.body: Nakiyemba Grace, 24, has waited while staff finish immunizations. She looks tired but is walking and talking normally.
coach.quote: “I have had fever for three days, nurse. My head is paining me.”

teach.label: Before you anchor on malaria
teach.text: Fever for three days is common — your first job is to decide how sick she is. Let the vitals and a quick danger-sign screen answer that before you treat.

critical.title: Fever ≥ 38 °C with headache · screen for danger signs
critical.body: Tachycardia may reflect fever. Re-check temperature and mental status.

coach.title: Her vitals are in. What concerns you most?
coach.body: Read the strip on the left before you choose.

question.prompt: Which single finding most changes your urgency?
question.right: Fever ≥ 38 °C together with headache is the combination that should trigger a malaria danger-sign screen. HR 104 is likely from fever; BP and RR are reassuring.
question.wrong: HR, BP, and RR are not your main concern here. It is the fever (38.8 °C) paired with headache that should raise urgency — that pair is when you actively look for severe malaria features.

sections.title: Subjective
sections.text: 24F · 3-day intermittent fever and headache. Paracetamol at home with little relief.
sections.reveal_text: No vomiting everything, no convulsions, no confusion. Drinking normally. Denies pregnancy.

sections.title: Danger-sign screen
sections.reveal_note: No danger signs — safe for outpatient assessment

coach.title: You have one focused question first. Make it count.
coach.body: You will take a fuller history, but the first question should be the one that could change your plan fastest.

options.text: Screen for danger signs — convulsions, confusion, inability to drink, persistent vomiting
Ask which herbal medicines she has tried
Ask about family history of headache
Ask for her NHIS membership number

question.right: In a febrile adult, danger signs decide the setting of care — manage here, or stabilise and refer. Everything else can follow once you know she is safe to treat as an outpatient.
question.wrong: Those can wait. With fever and headache, your first question should rule danger signs in or out — they decide whether she stays or is referred. The others do not change your immediate plan.

coach.title: No danger signs. She is safe to manage here. Next?
coach.body: She is alert, drinking, not vomiting, and has no respiratory distress. Malaria is high on your list in this setting.

options.text: Order a malaria RDT and wait for the result before treating
Start artemether-lumefantrine now — it is almost certainly malaria
Give a broad-spectrum antibiotic to be safe
Send her home with paracetamol and review in 3 days

question.right: Test before you treat. Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 require parasitological confirmation (RDT or microscopy) before antimalarials where testing is available. It also protects against missing a non-malarial cause.
question.wrong: Presumptive treatment is what the test-before-treat rule exists to stop. Order the RDT first — antimalarials without a positive test waste medicine and can mask another diagnosis. Antibiotics are not indicated yet, and sending her home misses a treatable cause.

ai.headline: Confirmed malaria · weight 56 kg → AL 4 tabs/dose
ai.sub: Suggests AL 20/120, 4 tabs twice daily × 3 days. Confirm to prescribe.

coach.title: RDT: positive for P. falciparum
coach.body: The lab sends the result to the visit. Check the weight-based dose before you confirm the prescription.

teach.label: Who is deciding here
teach.text: The assistant proposes; you dispose. The prescription is only real once you confirm the dose band.

sections.title: Prescription
counselling: Finish all 6 doses, even when better
Return if vomiting, confusion, or fever persists > 48 h
Take with fatty food · keep fluids up

coach.title: Confirm the artemether-lumefantrine dose
coach.body: Grace weighs 56 kg. AL is dosed by weight band. Check before you confirm.

question.prompt: Which AL regimen is correct for a 56 kg adult?

options.text: 4 tablets (80/480 mg) twice daily for 3 days

question.right: For ≥ 35 kg, AL 20/120 is 4 tablets per dose, twice daily, for 3 days (24 tablets total). Counsel her to take it with fatty food and finish every dose even when she feels better.
question.wrong: Check the weight band. At ≥ 35 kg the dose is 4 tablets twice daily for 3 days — 24 tablets total. Under-dosing risks treatment failure; the course is always 3 days, twice daily.

sections.title: HMIS codes
sections.receipt:
HC III
NAKIYEMBA GRACE · PT-100024
DX: MALARIA (B54)
RX: AL 20/120 · 4 TABS BD × 3D

coach.title: One last step: the diagnosis code
coach.body: Choose the HMIS code that will appear on the receipt and in the monthly 105 report.

question.prompt: Which is the primary HMIS diagnosis?
question.right: With a positive RDT, the confirmed diagnosis is malaria — B54. Fever and headache were symptoms, not the diagnosis; coding them instead would understate malaria burden in the HMIS 105 report.
question.wrong: Once the RDT is positive, the diagnosis is malaria (B54) — not the symptoms that brought her in. Accurate coding is what makes the clinic's malaria numbers real in the monthly report.

sections.title: Visit summary
sections.text: Uncomplicated malaria after positive RDT, absent danger signs.
sections.emphasis: Refer urgently if severe malaria features develop.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: Danger-sign screen first, test before treat, weight-based AL, and code B54 after confirmation.

teach.text: Use the corrections box below if any step, dose, or referral threshold needs updating before CPD sign-off.
